name: Zen Buddhism
era: 6th century China; 12th century Japan to today
line: Sit, work and eat with full attention.

quote.text: To study the Buddha Way is to study the self. To study the self is to forget the self.

quotes.text: In the beginner’s mind there are many possibilities, but in the expert’s there are few.
Have you eaten your rice porridge? Then you had better wash your bowl.
My miraculous power and spiritual activity: drawing water and carrying firewood.
Do not seek to follow in the footsteps of the wise. Seek what they sought.
Before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water. After enlightenment, chop wood, carry water.

words.usage: Za is to sit, zen is meditation. The heart of the practice.
Sōtō practice: sitting with no object and no goal.
A story or question from the old masters that logic cannot settle.
Zhaozhou’s answer when asked if a dog has Buddha nature. The first kōan for many students.
Seeing things as they are. Not a possession and not an ending.
A first glimpse of awakening, to be deepened by practice.
Meeting each thing as if for the first time.
The mind not caught on anything; acting without the self in the way.
Sweeping, cooking and gardening done as meditation.
Slow walking between periods of sitting.
Literally, gathering the mind. Several days of near-continuous sitting.
You bow on entering and on leaving.
Sit on the front third so the knees can settle.
A gesture of respect and of two becoming one.
A title for a senior Zen teacher.
One of the three treasures, with Buddha and Dharma.

words.meaning: The teaching; the way things are
words.usage: Both what the Buddha taught and the truth it points to.
The set of nested bowls, and the formal way of eating from them.
Dōgen wrote that the role demands an awakened mind.
Where a student presents their understanding.
A presentation of the teaching, not a lecture about it.
A flat stick used on the shoulders to wake a drowsy sitter, often on request.
Breath and attention settle here in zazen.
Dōgen’s word for the mind in zazen: neither thinking nor suppressing thought.
Everything is passing. Dōgen: impermanence is itself Buddha nature.
Nothing has a fixed, separate self. Sanskrit: śūnyatā.
Brushed in a single stroke. It shows the mind of the moment it was made.

words.meaning: Beauty in the plain, worn and imperfect
words.usage: An aesthetic shaped by Zen and the tea ceremony.
From the way of tea: this gathering will never happen again.
Attention that stays after the action is finished.

words.meaning: A short verse recited during daily acts
words.usage: There are verses for waking, washing and eating.

words.meaning: One who vows to awaken with all beings
words.usage: The ideal of Mahāyāna Buddhism, to which Zen belongs.

practices.name: Zazen
practices.instructions: Sit on the front third of a firm cushion, or upright on a chair with your feet flat. Lengthen the spine, tuck the chin slightly, rest the left hand in the right with thumbs lightly touching. Keep the eyes half open, lowered to the floor a metre ahead. Breathe through the nose and count each out-breath from one to ten, then start again. When you notice you have drifted, return to one without comment. Do not move until the timer sounds.
practices.why: Dōgen called zazen the dharma gate of ease and joy and insisted it is not a means to awakening but awakening practiced. The posture itself is the teaching.
variations: Once counting is steady, drop it and simply follow the breath.
Shikantaza: no counting, no object. Just sit.
Two periods of fifteen minutes with five minutes of slow walking between.

practices.name: Samu
practices.instructions: Choose one physical task: sweep a floor, wash the dishes, weed a bed. Do it in silence with no audio and no hurry. Give the broom, the cloth or the bowl the same attention you gave the breath. When you finish, put every tool back where it lives.
practices.why: Baizhang’s rule for Chan monasteries: a day without work is a day without food. In Zen there is no line between practice and chores.
variations: Clean one thing nobody will notice.
Fifteen minutes of care for a shared space.

practices.name: Silent meal
practices.instructions: Eat one meal without speaking, reading or a screen. Pause before the first bite and consider where the food came from. Take modest portions and finish everything. Put your utensils down between mouthfuls. Wash your bowl as soon as you are done.
practices.why: Formal Zen meals, ōryōki, are eaten in silence from nested bowls that are wiped clean with tea or water, which is then drunk. Nothing is wasted.
variations: Recite a short verse of thanks before eating.
Eat with one bowl and one spoon.
Share a silent meal with someone.

practices.name: Tea and stillness
practices.instructions: Heat the water, warm the cup, make the tea and carry it to a quiet place. Hold the cup in both hands. Drink it while doing nothing else. When the cup is empty, sit for a few more breaths, then wash and dry it.
practices.why: Eisai brought tea seeds from China with Zen in 1191, partly to keep monks awake. The tea ceremony grew from that habit into a discipline of its own.
variations: Plain hot water, as monks often drink.
Sit outside with your tea and watch the light go.

rules.text: Do one thing at a time
rules.why: When walking, walk. When eating, eat. Divided attention is the habit this Onda is here to interrupt.
The first thing the mind meets sets its tone for the morning. Let it be silence.

rules.text: Eat in silence at one meal
rules.why: Silence lets a meal be a meal.

rules.text: Leave every space cleaner than you found it
rules.why: Care for a place is care for everyone who comes after you.
A grain of rice, a sheet of paper, a minute. Dōgen had the cook treat one leaf of greens as the body of the Buddha.
A small pause of respect, to the cushion, the meal, the work, marks it as practice.

customs.title: Bow at the door
customs.creator: Gasshō
customs.why: Bring the palms together on entering and leaving the place where you sit.

customs.title: Shoes off, placed neatly
customs.creator: At the threshold
customs.why: Toes pointing out, ready for whoever leaves next.

customs.title: Wipe your own bowl
customs.creator: Ōryōki

customs.title: Clean together
customs.creator: Sōji
customs.why: A short daily period when everyone cleans, teacher included.

customs.creator: Sōtō custom
customs.why: Sōtō students sit facing the wall, as Bodhidharma is said to have done for nine years.

customs.title: Walk between sittings
customs.creator: Kinhin

ethics.title: Do no harm
ethics.text: The first of the pure precepts. Before doing good, stop doing damage: in speech, in what you consume, in how you move through a room.
ethics.practice: Catch one unkind sentence today before it leaves your mouth.

ethics.title: The bodhisattva vow
ethics.text: Beings are numberless; I vow to free them. The vow is impossible on purpose. It turns practice outward.
ethics.practice: Dedicate this morning’s sitting to one person who is struggling.

ethics.title: Not wasting
ethics.text: Nothing is yours to squander. Use what you have fully and with respect, from water to time.
ethics.practice: Finish what is on your plate and what is on your desk.

ethics.title: Right speech
ethics.text: Speak what is true, useful and timely, and otherwise be quiet.
ethics.practice: Before speaking, ask: is it true, is it kind, is it needed?

ethics.title: Not praising self, not blaming others
ethics.text: One of the ten grave precepts. Both habits keep the self at the centre.
ethics.practice: Go a day without one self-promoting remark.

ethics.title: Gratitude for labour
ethics.text: The meal verse begins: innumerable labours brought us this food.
ethics.practice: Thank one person whose work you usually do not see.

philosophy.title: Just this
philosophy.text: Nothing is missing from this moment. The search for something better is the only thing in the way.
philosophy.practice: Stop once an hour and name what is actually here.

philosophy.title: Beginner’s mind
philosophy.text: Meet each task as if for the first time, without the weight of what you already know.
philosophy.practice: Do one familiar thing today as if you had never done it.

philosophy.title: Practice and awakening are one
philosophy.text: Dōgen: you do not sit in order to become a Buddha. Sitting is what a Buddha does.
philosophy.practice: Sit today with no goal for the sitting.

philosophy.title: No separate self
philosophy.text: Look for the one who is looking. What you call the self is a stream, not a thing.
philosophy.practice: When irritated, ask quietly: who is it that is offended?

philosophy.title: Impermanence
philosophy.text: Everything that begins, ends. Seen clearly this is not sad; it is why anything can happen at all.
philosophy.practice: Watch one thing finish today: a cup of tea, a conversation, the light.

philosophy.title: Form is emptiness
philosophy.text: From the Heart Sutra. Things exist, but not on their own: each is made of everything else.
philosophy.practice: Hold a piece of bread and trace it back: baker, wheat, rain, sun.

philosophy.title: Not knowing
philosophy.text: A Chinese master said: not knowing is most intimate. Certainty closes the door that attention opens.
philosophy.practice: In one conversation, ask instead of telling.

philosophy.title: Ordinary mind is the Way
philosophy.text: Awakening is not somewhere else. It is washing the bowl, completely.
philosophy.practice: Choose your dullest chore and give it everything.

philosophy.title: The great doubt
philosophy.text: Rinzai teachers say: great doubt, great awakening. Hold the question; do not rush to fill it.
philosophy.practice: Carry one question all day without answering it.

philosophy.title: One time, one meeting
philosophy.text: This meeting, with this person, in this light, will not come again.
philosophy.practice: Give the next person you meet your whole attention for two minutes.

journal: When were you fully present today, and when were you elsewhere?
What did you do with complete attention?
What did you cling to that you could have let pass?
Describe one ordinary moment in detail.
What did silence show you?
Where did you rush, and what were you rushing toward?
What did you notice today for the first time?
What happened in your body during zazen?
Which thought came back most often on the cushion?
What did you do today that needed no improvement?
Where did you add a story to a plain fact?
What did you waste?
What did the work of your hands teach you?
Who did you meet as if for the first time?
What ended today?
When did you want the moment to be different from what it was?
What did the meal taste like?
What were you sure of this morning that you are less sure of now?
Where did you seek praise?
What sound did you hear when you stopped?
What would be different if there were nothing to attain?
Whose labour did you depend on today?
What question are you carrying?
When did you act before thinking, and it was right?
What did you clean, and how did it feel to finish?
What are you holding that is already gone?
Where was the self loudest today?
What would a beginner have seen that you missed?
What was enough?
Write three lines about this evening. Do not explain them.
reflect: What did sitting still reveal that moving had hidden?
Which practice changed you the most, and why?
Where did you resist, and what was the resistance protecting?
What does "just this" mean to you now?
What will you keep doing without counting it?

guide.era: 6th century China; 12th century Japan to today
intro: Zen is a school of Buddhism built around one act: sitting down, being still and seeing directly. It distrusts explanations, including its own.

The name tells the story of its journey. The Sanskrit word for meditation, dhyāna, became chan in China and zen in Japan. Tradition traces the school to Bodhidharma, an Indian monk said to have arrived in China around the year 520 and to have sat facing a cave wall for nine years. Whatever the history behind the legend, a distinctive Chinese school had formed by the eighth century, shaped as much by Daoist plainness as by Indian scripture.

Its early masters taught by encounter rather than lecture: a shout, a question turned back on the asker, a bowl to be washed. These exchanges were collected and became kōans, cases that a student sits with until the reasoning mind gives up and something else answers. A four-line verse attributed to the school sums up its claim: a special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words, pointing directly at the mind, seeing one’s nature and becoming Buddha.

Two Japanese monks carried the practice home. Eisai returned from China in 1191 with the Rinzai school and with tea. Dōgen returned in 1227 with the Sōtō school and a single instruction, shikantaza: just sit. Rinzai trains with kōans and sudden breakthrough. Sōtō holds that sitting itself is awakening and that nothing needs to be added. Both run monasteries where sitting, chanting, cooking and sweeping are one continuous practice.

Because Zen treats every activity as practice, it soaked into Japanese culture well beyond the temple: ink painting, the dry garden, the tea ceremony, haiku, archery, the taste for things plain and weathered. In the twentieth century it travelled west through the books of D. T. Suzuki and through teachers such as Shunryū Suzuki, who opened a small sitting group in San Francisco in 1959.

This Onda borrows the daily shape of lay Zen practice: sit in the morning, work with attention, eat one meal in silence, end the day with tea. Zen is a living religious tradition, and nothing here replaces a teacher or a community. If the sitting takes hold, find a local group and sit with them.

figures.name: Bodhidharma
figures.bio: The semi-legendary Indian monk counted as the first patriarch of Chan in China.

figures.name: Huineng
figures.bio: The Sixth Patriarch. By tradition an illiterate woodcutter who awakened on hearing a line of the Diamond Sutra.

figures.name: Zhaozhou
figures.bio: Tang master of the plain reply: "Mu", "Wash your bowl", "Have some tea".

figures.name: Linji
figures.bio: Fierce Tang master whose line became Rinzai Zen.

figures.name: Eisai
figures.bio: Brought Rinzai Zen and tea cultivation from China to Japan. Founded Kennin-ji in Kyoto.

figures.name: Dōgen
figures.bio: Founder of Sōtō Zen in Japan and of Eihei-ji. Author of the Shōbōgenzō.

figures.name: Ikkyū
figures.bio: Poet, abbot and scourge of pious hypocrisy.

figures.name: Sen no Rikyū
figures.bio: Tea master who gave the tea ceremony its austere, rustic form.

figures.name: Hakuin
figures.bio: Reviver of Rinzai. Organised kōan training and asked for the sound of one hand.

figures.name: Ryōkan
figures.bio: Hermit monk and poet who called himself the Great Fool.

figures.name: D. T. Suzuki
figures.bio: Scholar whose English books introduced Zen to the West.

figures.name: Shunryū Suzuki
figures.bio: Sōtō priest who founded San Francisco Zen Center and Tassajara.

history.what: Bodhidharma is said to arrive in China
history.detail: The earliest records are thin and the details are legend, but the story of nine years facing a wall at Shaolin set the tone for the school.
The Platform Sutra, composed in his name, argues that awakening is sudden and available to anyone, lettered or not.

history.what: The Tang golden age of Chan
history.detail: Mazu, Zhaozhou, Linji and Dongshan teach by direct encounter. Baizhang is credited with the first monastic rules for Chan, including daily work.

history.what: The Blue Cliff Record is compiled
history.detail: Yuanwu’s collection of one hundred kōans with commentary. A century later Wumen assembles the shorter Gateless Gate in 1228.

history.what: Eisai returns to Japan with Rinzai Zen
history.detail: He also brings tea seeds and later writes a treatise on drinking tea for health.
He writes Universal Recommendations for Zazen almost at once: the first Japanese instructions for sitting.
The temple of eternal peace, deep in the mountains of Echizen. It is still one of the two head temples of Sōtō Zen.

history.what: Zen shapes the arts of Kyoto
history.detail: Under shogunal patronage Zen temples become centres of ink painting, garden design and poetry. Ryōan-ji’s rock garden dates from the end of this period.
The tea master, ordered to take his own life by the warlord Hideyoshi, leaves behind the wabi style of tea.

history.what: Bashō sets out for the north
history.detail: His five-month walk becomes The Narrow Road to the Deep North.
From a poor country temple he trains a generation of teachers and arranges kōans into a graded course still used today.
The Rinzai abbot Shaku Sōen speaks at the World’s Parliament of Religions. His student D. T. Suzuki translates.

history.what: D. T. Suzuki publishes Essays in Zen Buddhism
history.detail: The first of the books that introduce Zen to English readers.

history.what: Shunryū Suzuki arrives in San Francisco
history.detail: Americans begin joining his dawn sittings. San Francisco Zen Center is incorporated in 1962 and opens Tassajara, a mountain monastery, in 1967.

concepts.text: Seated meditation: the core of the practice.
concepts.detail: Upright, still, eyes lowered, breathing naturally. In Sōtō it is done facing a wall with no object. In Rinzai it is often done holding a kōan.

concepts.text: A recorded exchange used as an object of meditation.
concepts.detail: A kōan is not a riddle with a clever answer. The student holds it until the habit of standing outside and analysing falls away, then shows the teacher what is left.
Rinzai emphasises a breakthrough experience; Sōtō is wary of chasing one. Both agree that an insight not lived out in ordinary conduct is worth little.
Emptiness is not nothingness. It means that every thing depends on everything else and has no fixed core, which is exactly why change and compassion are possible.

concepts.text: Every being already has the capacity for awakening.
concepts.detail: Dōgen went further and read the phrase as: all beings are Buddha nature. Practice does not create it. Practice expresses it.

concepts.text: The teaching passes from teacher to student, mind to mind.
concepts.detail: Zen lineages are written as family trees back to the Buddha. The early links are legend, but the insistence on a living teacher is real.

concepts.text: The two main schools of Japanese Zen.
concepts.detail: Rinzai: kōans, vigorous training, close work with a teacher. Sōtō: shikantaza, just sitting, and attention to the forms of daily life. A smaller third school, Ōbaku, arrived in the seventeenth century.
Chan monasteries supported themselves by farming, unlike the alms-based monasteries of India. Work was folded into the meditation schedule and stayed there.

concepts.text: The beauty of the modest and the worn.
concepts.detail: Wabi is spare simplicity; sabi is the patina of age. The tea masters prized a cracked bowl over a perfect one.
Sixteen in the Sōtō tradition: three refuges, three pure precepts and ten grave precepts, from not killing to not disparaging the three treasures.

facts.text: Zen, chan, sŏn and thiền are the Japanese, Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese readings of one character, which renders the Sanskrit dhyāna, meditation.
Dōgen was twenty-three when he sailed to China. An old monastery cook, drying mushrooms in the midday sun, taught him that the kitchen was practice too.
The rock garden at Ryōan-ji holds fifteen stones, arranged so that at least one is always hidden from wherever you sit on the veranda.
Eisai’s treatise Drinking Tea for Health opens by calling tea an elixir for nourishing life.
Hakuin’s best-known kōan is: you know the sound of two hands clapping. What is the sound of one hand?
In a Zen monastery the cook, the tenzo, is one of the six senior officers and is expected to be a mature practitioner.
Legend says Bodhidharma cut off his own eyelids to stay awake, and that the first tea plants grew where they fell.
Steve Jobs studied with the Sōtō priest Kōbun Chino Otogawa, who also officiated at his wedding.

glossary.meaning: The Chinese school from which Japanese Zen descends.
The school of just sitting, brought to Japan by Dōgen.
The school of kōan training, brought to Japan by Eisai.
Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, Dōgen’s life work.
A very short scripture on emptiness, chanted daily in Zen temples.
Buddha, Dharma and Sangha: the teacher, the teaching and the community.

sensitivity.note: Zen is a living Buddhist tradition. This Onda adapts its everyday lay practices. It is not ordination, and it does not replace a teacher or a community.
requiredCaveats: Sitting through pain is not the goal: adjust your posture or use a chair.
If meditation brings up distress that does not settle, stop and speak to a qualified teacher or clinician.
